title: Getting Started
text:
GeoLattice needs Python 3.10 or newer (tested on 3.11 and 3.14; its dependencies need 3.10, for example libpysal 4.10). GDAL and PROJ must be installed first, with Python GDAL bindings that match the GDAL library; install them with conda or your system package manager.
Then install GeoLattice from PyPI:
python3 -m pip install geolattice
Installing GeoLattice installs every runtime dependency listed in requirements.txt, whether you install from PyPI, the wheel or the sdist (pip install dist/geolattice-0.3.49-cp314-cp314-linux_x86_64.whl or pip install dist/geolattice-0.3.49.tar.gz). That list is the conflict-free set that installation option 6 (geolattice[all]) resolves to: about 80 packages, including PyTorch. pip install -r requirements.txt installs the same set without GeoLattice itself.


The option names below still work, and existing install commands keep working, but a plain install already includes all of them. Each option includes everything in the one above it.








Option
Install
Adds




1. Core
geolattice[core]
Vector and raster I/O including GeoParquet, CRS tools, maps and plots (rasterio, fiona, GeoPandas, pyarrow, matplotlib, folium, contextily, plotly)


2. Spatial analysis
geolattice[analysis]
Terrain and hydrology, suitability, multidimensional rasters, network and segregation analysis (xarray, netCDF4, zarr, dask, networkx, OSMnx, libpysal, WhiteboxTools)


3. Spatial statistics
geolattice[statistics]
ESDA, spatial weights, GWR, point patterns, spatial regression, and spatial causal inference (scikit-learn, joblib)


4. Geostatistics
geolattice[geostats]
Variograms, kriging and simulation, with plotting helpers


5. Remote sensing
geolattice[remote-sensing]
Optical, SAR, lidar, hyperspectral and UAV processing, STAC access, classification (rioxarray, scikit-image, pystac-client, laspy, h5py, OpenCV, xgboost, leafmap)


6. All
geolattice[all]
Everything above plus web and cloud GIS, spatial databases, deep learning (PyTorch, torchgeo), Bayesian models (PyMC), boosting, JAX kriging, Earth Engine and distributed computing (Dask, dask-geopandas)



python3 -m pip install "geolattice[core]"             # 1. core, vector, raster, CRS, visualization
python3 -m pip install "geolattice[analysis]"         # 2. core + spatial analysis
python3 -m pip install "geolattice[statistics]"       # 3. core + spatial analysis + spatial statistics
python3 -m pip install "geolattice[geostats]"         # 4. ... + geostatistics
python3 -m pip install "geolattice[remote-sensing]"   # 5. ... + remote sensing
python3 -m pip install "geolattice[all]"              # 6. all
A few groups need special hardware or conflict with other packages, so neither a plain install nor geolattice[all] includes them; add them by name when you need them: compute, geostatistics-gpu and rsense-gpu (CUDA GPUs), geostatistics-h2o and geostatistics-tensorflow, rsense-uav-dl, rsense-vision and rsense-foundation (large vision and foundation models), rsense-biopar (needs pandas below 3), distributed-gpu (CUDA GPUs), distributed-hpc (SLURM, PBS and Kubernetes clusters), distributed-spark (Apache Sedona, needs Java 17 or newer) and dev. When a function needs a library that is not installed, its error message names the extra and the installation option that contains it.
For a GPU, see GPU support below.



GeoLattice includes a small C extension, so building it needs a C compiler and NumPy. From the repository root:
python3 -m pip install build
python3 -m build
python3 -m pip install dist/geolattice-0.3.49-cp314-cp314-linux_x86_64.whl   # installs every dependency in requirements.txt
python3 -m build writes an sdist and a wheel for the Python that ran it (cp314 above). For another Python version, build a wheel from the sdist with that Python: python3 -m pip wheel --no-deps -w dist dist/geolattice-0.3.49.tar.gz. For development, install in editable mode with python3 -m pip install -e ".[dev]".
The user guide lists the 65 individual extras the installation options are built from and explains how to fix the common GDAL import errors (libgdal.so not found, No module named '_gdal').



The package was renamed from PyGIS to GeoLattice. Existing code keeps working for now, but should move to the new names:







PyGIS
GeoLattice




pip install pygis, pygis[all]
pip install geolattice, geolattice[all]


import pygis, from pygis.raster import ...
import geolattice, from geolattice.raster import ...


pygis.pygisdb, pygis.spatial_bd.pygisdb
geolattice.geolatticedb, geolattice.spatial_bd.geolatticedb


PYGIS_EXPLORER, PYGIS_FTW_CACHE, PYGIS_SEDONA_PACKAGES, PYGIS_UAV_WEIGHTS
GEOLATTICE_EXPLORER, GEOLATTICE_FTW_CACHE, GEOLATTICE_SEDONA_PACKAGES, GEOLATTICE_UAV_WEIGHTS


Model cache ~/.cache/pygis/
~/.cache/geolattice/




Uninstall the old package first (python3 -m pip uninstall pygis), because GeoLattice installs its own pygis alias.
The alias makes import pygis and from pygis.x import y return the geolattice modules, with a FutureWarning. It will be removed in a future release.
The old PYGIS_ environment variables are no longer read; rename them in your shell profile or job scripts.
To keep model weights you have already downloaded, move the cache folder: mv ~/.cache/pygis ~/.cache/geolattice.

title: Getting Started
text:
Quick start
Run these examples from the repository root. They use the sample data in Data/00_shared and need installation option 5 (geolattice[remote-sensing]).
from pathlib import Path

DATA = Path("Data/00_shared")  # sample data in the repository

# Vector: read US counties, reproject New York to metres and buffer each county by 5 km
from geolattice.vector import buffer, read_vector_data

with read_vector_data(DATA / "vector_data/USA/US_COUNTY.shp") as layer:
    counties = layer.to_dataframe()  # GeoDataFrame with 3,108 counties
ny = counties[counties["STATE"] == "New York"].to_crs(5070)  # CONUS Albers, metres
zones = buffer(ny, 5_000)

# Raster and terrain: summary statistics, slope and hillshade of a DEM
from geolattice.raster import summarize_raster
from geolattice.spatial_analysis import hillshade, slope

dem = DATA / "raster_data/USA/Onondaga_DEM.tif"
print(summarize_raster(dem)["mean"])
slope(dem, "slope.tif", units="degrees", overwrite=True)
hillshade(dem, "hillshade.tif", azimuth=315, altitude=45)

# Geostatistics: variogram and ordinary kriging of log zinc in the Meuse data
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from geolattice.geostatistics import OrdinaryKriging, Variogram

meuse = pd.read_csv(DATA / "data_geostatistics/meuse.csv")
xy, z = meuse[["x", "y"]].to_numpy(), np.log(meuse["zinc"].to_numpy())
vgm = Variogram(xy, z, model="spherical", n_lags=12)
vgm.fit()
ok = OrdinaryKriging(vgm).fit(xy, z)
print(ok.predict(np.array([[179500.0, 331500.0]])))

# Remote sensing: NDVI from Landsat 9 surface reflectance
import xarray as xr
import geolattice.rsense as rs

scene = DATA / "data_remote_sensing/landsat9_vegas_20240708/LC09_L2SP_039035_20240708_02_T1"
bands = xr.Dataset({b: rs.read(scene / f"{b}.tif").squeeze("band", drop=True) for b in ("red", "nir")})
bands.attrs["pyrsense:sensor"] = "landsat"  # tells GeoLattice which scaling rules apply
ndvi = bands.rs.scale().rs.index("NDVI")  # scale to reflectance, then compute NDVI
print(float(ndvi.mean()))

# Foundation models: embed a raster with DOFA, then find chips that look like the first one
import geolattice.rsense.foundation_models as fm  # needs geolattice[rsense-foundation]

fm.recommend("soil")                          # AlphaEarth, Clay, Presto, SSL4EO
enc = fm.load_model("dofa-base", bands=["red", "nir"])
emb = enc.embed_raster(bands.rs.scale().to_dataarray("band"), chip_size=224)
sim = fm.similarity_map(emb, emb.isel(y=0, x=0))

# Evapotranspiration: METRIC on a Landsat scene (sr: scaled reflectance, lst: surface temperature in K)
import geolattice.rsense.surface_energy_balance as seb

ndvi, lai = seb.ndvi(sr.red, sr.nir), seb.leaf_area_index(seb.savi(sr.red, sr.nir, L=0.1))
alb, e0 = seb.albedo(sr, sensor="landsat8"), seb.surface_emissivity(lai, ndvi)
anchors = seb.select_anchors(ndvi, lst, albedo_=alb)          # hot and cold pixels (Allen et al. 2013)
rs_in = seb.incoming_shortwave(cos_theta=0.92, tau_sw=0.78)   # clear-sky shortwave at overpass
rl_in = seb.incoming_longwave(anchors["cold"]["lst"], seb.air_emissivity(tau_sw=0.78))
rn = seb.net_radiation(rs_in, alb, rl_in, seb.outgoing_longwave(lst, e0), e0)
g = seb.soil_heat_flux(rn, lst, lai=lai, method="metric")
et = seb.run_metric(lst, rn, g, seb.momentum_roughness(lai=lai), seb.wind_at_blending_height(2.5),
                    100.6, etr_inst=0.93, anchors=anchors, etr_daily=12.0)   # Dataset: h, le, etrf, et24

# Soil moisture physics: soil water limits, L-band permittivity, brightness temperature and its inversion
import geolattice.rsense.soil_moisture as sm

soil = sm.saxton_rawls(sand=0.40, clay=0.20)            # loam: WP 0.14, FC 0.28, saturation 0.46 m3/m3
eps = sm.mironov_dielectric(0.25, clay=0.20)             # 13.0 - 1.5j at 1.41 GHz
tb = sm.tau_omega(295.0, eps, 40.0, tau=0.3, pol="v")    # 260.7 K
theta = sm.invert_tau_omega(tb, 295.0, 40.0, clay=0.20, tau=0.3)   # back to 0.25 m3/m3
The user guide has worked examples for every module, including the full raster toolset, hydrology, suitability analysis, geostatistical simulation, SAR and InSAR processing, lidar, hyperspectral analysis, image classification, evapotranspiration from the surface energy balance and soil moisture physics.

title: Getting Started
text:
GPU support
GeoLattice runs on the CPU by default. On a machine with an NVIDIA GPU, the parts below can run on the GPU, and they fall back to the CPU when no usable GPU is found.








Module
GPU library
How to use it




geolattice.geostatistics: variograms, kriging, cross-validation and sequential, turning bands, direct sequential and multiple-point simulation
CuPy
use_gpu=True on the class or function


geolattice.geostatistics.jax_variogram_kriging: simple, ordinary, universal and cokriging
JAX
use_gpu="auto"


geolattice.rsense: raster cubes, indices, composites and other array operations
CuPy (NVIDIA) or PyTorch MPS (Apple)
rs.backend.set_backend("cuda") or "mps"


geolattice.rsense.dl, geolattice.rsense.classify, geolattice.rsense.foundation_models: deep learning, image classification, segmentation, detection and foundation model embeddings
PyTorch
runs on the GPU when PyTorch sees one


geolattice.spatial_statistics: GNNWR and GTNNWR
PyTorch
device="cuda" or "auto"


geolattice.distributed: raster algebra, focal filters and terrain, vector measures, point-in-polygon joins, nearest neighbours, zonal statistics, spatial statistics, clustering, networks, flow direction and model prediction
CuPy, cuDF, cuML, cuGraph, PyTorch
compute="gpu" or "auto" on each function



import numpy as np
from geolattice.geostatistics import OrdinaryKriging, Variogram
from geolattice.geostatistics.utils.backend import cupy_gpu_usable

print(cupy_gpu_usable())  # True when CuPy can run a kernel on the GPU

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
xy = rng.uniform(0, 100, size=(200, 2))
z = np.sin(xy[:, 0] / 20) + rng.normal(0, 0.1, size=200)
grid = np.stack(np.meshgrid(np.linspace(0, 100, 300), np.linspace(0, 100, 300)), -1).reshape(-1, 2)

vgm = Variogram(xy, z, model="spherical", n_lags=12, use_gpu=True)
vgm.fit()
pred = OrdinaryKriging(vgm, use_gpu=True).fit(xy, z).predict(grid)  # 90,000 cells on the GPU

import geolattice.rsense as rs

rs.backend.set_backend("cuda")  # rsense arrays now live on the GPU as CuPy arrays
print(rs.backend.get_backend())
rs.backend.set_backend("cpu")
The GPU extras (compute, geostatistics-gpu and rsense-gpu) install cupy-cuda13x, the CuPy build for CUDA 13. Check your CUDA version with nvidia-smi. For an older CUDA, install the matching CuPy yourself (cupy-cuda12x or cupy-cuda11x) together with geolattice[geostats] or geolattice[remote-sensing] instead of a GPU extra, and keep only one CuPy package in an environment, because they all provide the same cupy module. PyTorch and JAX choose their CUDA build at install time, so install them by following their own instructions; geolattice[all] installs the default PyTorch build from PyPI.

title: Getting Started
text:
Distributed computing
geolattice.distributed gives one API for spatial data that scales from all cores of a laptop to a cluster. Every function takes compute="auto" | "cpu" | "gpu" and returns the type and memory space it was given; Dask-backed input stays lazy. Without a cluster it runs on Dask’s threads, so it already uses every CPU core.
import geolattice.distributed as pdist

with pdist.start("cuda"):                                  # one Dask worker per GPU ("local" for CPU)
    dem = pdist.read_raster("dem.tif")                     # lazy and chunked
    slope = pdist.raster.slope(dem, compute="gpu")         # CuPy chunks with a 1-pixel halo
    stats = pdist.zonal_stats(parcels, slope)              # per-chunk partial sums, combined at the end
    hits = pdist.vector.sjoin(points, parcels, predicate="within")   # GPU point-in-polygon test
    w = pdist.analysis.weights(parcels, "queen")
    lisa = pdist.analysis.local_morans(stats["mean"], w)  # 999 permutations as batched matrix products
    pdist.write_raster(slope, "slope.zarr")







Module
What it does




raster
Map algebra (calc, where, reclassify), focal filters, convolution and terrain (slope, aspect, hillshade, curvature, TPI, TRI, roughness), chunk by chunk with halos so results equal whole-array results


vector
Geometry operations, clip, sjoin on spatially partitioned data (Dask, GPU or Sedona engine), knn


bridge
rasterize, zonal_stats, extract_values, polygonize (polygons cut by chunk seams are merged)


analysis
Spatial weights, Moran’s I, Geary’s C, LISA, Getis-Ord G*, DBSCAN, HDBSCAN, k-means and kernel density


network
Graphs from lines, shortest paths, centrality and components (cuGraph or SciPy and NetworkX)


hydrology
Chunked D8 flow direction, depression filling and flow accumulation


ml
Model fitting, per-pixel raster prediction, tiled PyTorch inference over several GPUs and DDP training


io
Parallel GeoParquet and OGR reading and writing, rasters, Zarr and STAC


diagnostics
benchmark, check_equivalence (CPU against GPU), explain, memory_report, profile



pdist.start also connects to SLURM, PBS and Kubernetes clusters (geolattice[distributed-hpc]) or an existing scheduler, and vector.sjoin(..., engine="sedona") runs the join as Spark SQL (geolattice[distributed-spark]). Results are checked against GeoPandas, rasterio, scipy.ndimage, libpysal, esda and NetworkX in the test suite. Measured on an RTX A5500 laptop GPU:








Operation
CPU
GPU




Focal median 7 x 7, 8000 x 8000 DEM
17.5 s
0.24 s


Moran’s I, 22,500 cells, 999 permutations
0.71 s
0.07 s


Local Moran’s I, 22,500 cells, 999 permutations
1.55 s
0.25 s

0.82 s
0.22 s


Point-in-polygon join, 2 million points, 2,000 polygons
5.4 s (geopandas: 15.4 s)
4.7 s



Where the GPU version is slower on typical inputs (rasterize, dbscan), compute="auto" keeps the CPU; pdist.explain("bridge.rasterize") says which implementation runs and why. The user guide has worked examples.

geolattice.spatial_statistics.interpolate.IndicatorKriging
Ordinary indicator kriging. Methods: etype, fit, predict, predict_grid.


geolattice.spatial_statistics.interpolate.Interpolator

geolattice.spatial_statistics.interpolate.MultivariateCokriging
Ordinary cokriging of a primary variable with any number of secondaries. Methods: fit, predict, predict_grid.

geolattice.spatial_statistics.interpolate.ThinPlateSpline
Thin-plate spline: the smooth surface of minimum bending energy through the samples. Methods: clone, fit, get_params, predict, predict_grid.


geolattice.spatial_statistics.interpolate.TIN
Piecewise-linear interpolation on the Delaunay triangulation (a TIN surface). Methods: clone, fit, get_params, predict, predict_grid.


geolattice.spatial_statistics.interpolate.TrendSurface
Global polynomial trend surface of total degree degree. Methods: clone, fit, get_params, predict, predict_grid.


geolattice.spatial_statistics.interpolate.UniversalKriging

geolattice.spatial_statistics.interpolate.VariogramModel
Parametric semivariogram γ(h) = nugget + psill · g(h / range) for h > 0 (γ(0) = 0). Methods: gamma, plot, sill.

Cross-semivariogram γ̂₁₂(h) = 1/(2 N(h)) Σ (z₁ᵢ − z₁ⱼ)(z₂ᵢ − z₂ⱼ).

Matheron’s classical estimator γ̂(h) = 1/(2 N(h)) Σ (z_i - z_j)² in equal-width distance bins.

Sort quantile-regression predictions so a lower quantile stays below a higher one.


geolattice.spatial_statistics.interpolate.etype_estimate
E-type (conditional expectation) from indicator-kriging probabilities.


geolattice.spatial_statistics.interpolate.fit_cross_variogram
Least-squares fit of a cross-variogram.


geolattice.spatial_statistics.interpolate.fit_indicator_variogram

Try every combination of param_grid and rank by cross-validated metric.


geolattice.spatial_statistics.interpolate.indicator_transform
Code a continuous sample as an indicator.


geolattice.spatial_statistics.interpolate.make_grid
Regular grid over a region.

Thin-plate spline (an RBF with the thin-plate kernel).

Thiessen (Voronoi) polygons: one cell per sample, containing every location closer to that sample than to any other.

Name
Description

Name
Description

Coordinates (N, 2) of a sampling frame: ndarray, DataFrame with x/y, or GeoDataFrame.

Conditioned Latin hypercube sampling (Minasny & McBratney 2006).

Geometric quality of a sample: balance (Stevens-Olsen B), mean_dist_to_sample and max_dist_to_sample (from every frame unit to its nearest sampled unit, the quantity a kriging-oriented design tries to minimise) and min_spacing…

deff = Var(design) / Var(SRS of the same size): < 1 means the design is more efficient.

Local-mean variance estimator of the Horvitz-Thompson total Σ z_i (z_i = y_i / π_i) for spatially balanced samples (Stevens & Olsen 2003; Grafström & Schelin 2014).

Optimal (Neyman) allocation n_h ∝ N_h σ_h with a floor and largest-remainder rounding.

Sample size to estimate a mean to within ± margin at confidence conf: n0 = deff · (z σ / margin)² with the finite-population correction n = n0 / (1 + n0/N).


geolattice.spatial_statistics.sampling.simple_random
Simple random sample without replacement: π_i = n / N.


geolattice.spatial_statistics.sampling.space_filling
Purposive design that covers the study area evenly (for model-based inference, e.g. choosing monitoring sites for kriging).


geolattice.spatial_statistics.sampling.spatial_balance
Stevens-Olsen (2004) spatial balance statistic B.


geolattice.spatial_statistics.sampling.spatial_order
Permutation that orders units along a space-filling path (‘hilbert’) or an axis (‘x’, ‘y’).


geolattice.spatial_statistics.sampling.stratified
Stratified random sample.


geolattice.spatial_statistics.sampling.systematic
Systematic sample from a frame ordered along a path: pick a random start and then every k = N/n-th unit.

Two-stage cluster sample: n_clusters primary units (e.g. counties) drawn by SRS, then n_per_cluster units by SRS inside each (all units if the cluster is smaller).

Result of local_moran_clusters. Methods: get, plot, stats, summary, to_frame.

Attributes ———- labels : ndarray (n,) cluster id (0, 1, …) or -1 for noise summary_frame : DataFrame per-cluster size, centroid, hull area and density Methods: get, plot, stats, summary, to_frame.

Description

Contiguity-constrained hierarchical clustering: at each step only adjacent clusters may merge (the neighbour graph w is the connectivity constraint).

Pairwise Jaccard indices between named boolean masks (e.g. ’Gi*’ hot spots vs ‘LISA’ HH clusters).

title: API Reference
text:
Geostatistics
Variograms, kriging, simulation, cross-validation and GSLIB-style helpers, on CPU, GPU (CuPy) or JAX.
import geolattice.geostatistics

geolattice.geostatistics.core
Core geostatistical components: variogram estimation, theoretical models, and kriging.
Classes







Name
Description




geolattice.geostatistics.OrdinaryKriging
Ordinary Kriging with GPU support (CuPy) and block kriging option. Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.SimpleKriging
Simple Kriging with known mean. Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.Variogram
Signature: Variogram(coords, values, model='spherical', estimator='matheron', maxlag=None, n_lags=10, anisotropy=None, use_gpu='auto'). Methods: fit, set_params.


geolattice.geostatistics.VariogramCloud
Container for variogram cloud data (pairwise dist, gamma, and point-pair indices). Methods: from_coords, point_pairs.



Functions







Name
Description




geolattice.geostatistics.compute_variogram_cloud
Compute the variogram cloud: all pairwise distances and semivariances.


geolattice.geostatistics.covariance_from_variogram
Covariance C(h) from variogram: C(h) = C(0) - γ(h), with C(0) = nugget + sill.


geolattice.geostatistics.cubic
Cubic variogram (Chilès & Delfiner / gstat).


geolattice.geostatistics.exponential
Signature: exponential(h, nugget, sill, range_).


geolattice.geostatistics.fit_indicator_variogram
Fit empirical indicator variogram and return lags, gamma.


geolattice.geostatistics.gaussian
Signature: gaussian(h, nugget, sill, range_).


geolattice.geostatistics.matern
Signature: matern(h, nugget, sill, range_, nu=1.5).


geolattice.geostatistics.plot_variogram_cloud
Plot variogram cloud (distance vs semivariance) and optionally identify or digitize point pairs.


geolattice.geostatistics.spherical
Signature: spherical(h, nugget, sill, range_).


geolattice.geostatistics.stable
Signature: stable(h, nugget, sill, range_, alpha=1.0).





geolattice.geostatistics.jax_variogram_kriging
JAX variograms and kriging for CPU and GPU.

Name
Description

Ordinary cokriging of one primary and one secondary variable. Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.JaxOrdinaryKriging
Ordinary kriging on a JAX device (CPU or GPU). Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.JaxSimpleKriging
Simple kriging with a known mean. Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.JaxUniversalKriging
Universal kriging with a polynomial drift. Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.JaxVariogram
Empirical variogram and a fitted theoretical model, evaluated with JAX. Methods: fit, set_params.





geolattice.geostatistics.ml
Regression kriging with machine-learning trend models.

Name
Description




geolattice.geostatistics.CNNLSTMRegressionKriging
Convolutional-LSTM trend model + per-time-step kriging of residuals, for a fixed set of monitoring locations observed repeatedly over time. Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.ConvLSTM
Convolutional LSTM (Shi, Chen, Wang, Yeung, Wong & Woo, 2015, https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.04214) + kriging of residuals. Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.DCRNN
Diffusion Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (Li, Yi, Shahabi & Liu, 2018, https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.01926) + kriging of residuals. Methods: fit, predict.

Deep Regression Kriging: a PyTorch MLP trend model + kriging of residuals. Methods: fit, plot_losses, plot_optuna_history, predict.

Deep Regression Kriging with TensorFlow/Keras for the trend model. Methods: fit, plot_losses, plot_optuna_history, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.GAMRegressor
scikit-learn-compatible wrapper around pyGAM <https://pygam.readthedocs.io>_, fitting a purely additive smooth-term model :math:f(X) = \beta_0 + \sum_j s_j(X_j) – one spline smooth per feature. Methods: fit, get_params, predict, set_params.


geolattice.geostatistics.GMAN
Graph Multi-Attention Network (Zheng, Fan, Wang & Qi, 2020, AAAI, https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.08415) + kriging of residuals. Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.GNNRegressionKriging
Plain spatial Graph Neural Network trend model + kriging of residuals. Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.IGNNK
Inductive Graph Neural Network for Kriging (Wu, Cui, Nie & Wang, 2021), adapted from its original spatiotemporal-sensor-network setting to static regression kriging, + kriging of residuals. Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.KCN
Kriging Convolutional Networks (Appleby, Liu & Liu, 2020) + kriging of residuals. Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.RegressionKriging
Regression Kriging = Regression + Kriging of Residuals. Methods: feature_importances_, fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.RegressionKrigingH2O
Regression Kriging with H2O-3 for the trend model. Methods: fit, get_best_model_metrics, predict, shutdown.


geolattice.geostatistics.STGNNRegressionKriging
Spatio-temporal graph neural network trend model + per-time-step kriging of residuals, for a fixed set of monitoring locations observed repeatedly over time. Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.STGTNRegressionKriging
Spatial-temporal graph Transformer trend model + per-time-step kriging of residuals, for a fixed set of monitoring locations observed repeatedly over time. Methods: fit, predict.

Spatial-Temporal Transformer Network (Xu, Dai, Liu, Gao, Lin, Qi & Xiong, 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02908) + kriging of residuals. Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.TGCN
Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (Zhao, Song, Zhang, Liu, Wang & Li, 2019, https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.05320) + kriging of residuals. Methods: fit, predict.



Functions







Name
Description




geolattice.geostatistics.enforce_quantile_monotonicity
Fix “quantile crossing”: given predictions from several independently fitted regressor='quantile' models (e.g. quantile levels 0.1, 0.5, 0.9) at the same locations, sort them point-by-point so a lower quantile is never predicted…





geolattice.geostatistics.kriging
Kriging estimators beyond ordinary / simple kriging (those live in core).
Classes







Name
Description




geolattice.geostatistics.AreaPoissonKriging
Area-to-area and area-to-point Poisson Kriging of block-support count/rate data, using each area’s actual point support (e.g. population points, see PointSupport) instead of a single representative centroid. Methods: fit, predict_area, predict_points.

Bayesian generalized linear kriging (spatial GLMM) by MCMC. Methods: fit, latent_samples, predict, predict_proba, predictive_samples.

Bayesian kriging with discrete priors on the range and the relative nugget and a conjugate normal-inverse-gamma prior on the trend and variance. Methods: fit, from_variogram, predict, predict_proba, predict_quantiles, predictive_samples, sample_parameters.


geolattice.geostatistics.BayesianTransformedKriging
Bayesian transformed Gaussian kriging (De Oliveira, Kedem & Short, 1997) for positive, skewed data: the Box-Cox parameter lambda joins the range and nugget-ratio grid. Methods: fit, from_variogram, predict, predict_proba, predict_quantiles, predictive_samples, sample_parameters.


geolattice.geostatistics.Cokriging
Ordinary cokriging (two unbiasedness constraints). Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.ColocatedCokriging

Empirical and theoretical cross-variogram. Methods: fit, fit_model, set_params.


geolattice.geostatistics.DisjunctiveKriging

geolattice.geostatistics.EmpiricalBayesianKriging
Empirical Bayesian Kriging: an ensemble of kriging models built from simulate-and-refit semivariograms, combined to propagate semivariogram-parameter uncertainty into the prediction variance and into a genuine mixture-of-Gaussians… Methods: fit, predict, predict_proba.

geolattice.geostatistics.IndicatorKriging
Ordinary Indicator Kriging with per-threshold variogram support. Methods: fit, predict.

geolattice.geostatistics.MultivariateCokriging
Ordinary full cokriging of a primary variable using one or more secondaries and an LMC. Methods: fit, predict.


geolattice.geostatistics.PointSupport
Groups point-support locations (e.g. census population points) by the area (block/polygon) they fall inside. Methods: centroid, coords, from_geodataframes, total, values.
